summary: Decide how to divide a system, how many deployments and quanta it has, its style, and its pieces.

blocks.title: Architecture styles compared
rows: Layered
Closed technical layers in one unit
Low
A feature change often touches every layer
Sinkholes, and layer rules that decay without checks
Modular monolith
Domain modules in one unit, a schema each
Low
All modules scale and fail together
Unchecked imports or a shared schema make a ball of mud
Microkernel
A core, plug-ins, a registry, one contract
Low
The plug-in contract is hard to change
The core grows by accident. A bad plug-in stops the core
Service-based
A UI, 4 to 12 coarse services, one shared database
Medium
The shared database is a shared point of failure
A slow database or a long query slows all services
Event-driven
A broker (no central part) or a mediator
High
The flow is hard to follow, test, and debug
Slow consumers, poison messages, silent stops
Microservices
One service for each bounded context, with its own data
High
High operating cost, hard cross-service transactions
Cascading failures, retry storms, data copies that drift
Space-based
Processing units with in-memory caches, data pumps to a database
High
Complex and expensive to build and operate
Data collisions, a pump backlog that grows
Pipeline
Filters and one-way pipes, usually one unit
Low
A poor fit for interactive work
One slow filter or one bad record stops the run

items.when: One set of characteristics fits all parts of the system
Parts need different characteristics, and you accept the network costs
items.use: A distributed style, after you find the quanta

items.when: The team is small, the budget is tight, or the problem is not yet clear
You want business boundaries without the cost of a distributed system
A stable core has many variations, such as one rule set per country
Business areas need some independence, and microservices cost too much
Work arrives in bursts, or one occurrence starts many independent reactions
Many teams, uneven load, and mature operations
Load peaks are extreme and hard to predict, such as a major ticket sale
The problem is one-way data processing: import, convert, enrich, export

blocks.title: Select a topology or a variant

items.when: An event flow is short, and new reactions are added often
An event flow has many steps, and the business must know when it completes
Service-based, and a schema change must not break every service
items.use: Partition the database and entity libraries by domain

items.when: One service-based service needs its own availability or scale
Space-based data is small and changes rarely, such as a venue map
items.use: A replicated cache in each unit

items.when: Space-based data is large, or has a high update rate, such as seat holds
Customers or partners write their own plug-ins
About 80% of the requests in a layered system are sinkholes
items.use: Vertical slices, or an open business layer

items.when: Modules need separate data, but one database to operate
items.use: A schema and a user per module

items.when: Dozens of services need the same logs, retries, and secure connections
items.use: A sidecar, or a service mesh

items.when: The business asks for changes in business terms
One word means different things to different people
Two areas must write the same table
One piece differs in load, change rate, uptime, security, or owner
items.use: Split it into its own part

items.when: Pieces share one transaction, call each other always, or change together
You need separate scale, fault isolation, separate releases, or different technology
You start a system and no reason to distribute is real yet
items.use: Modular monolith, then move modules out

items.when: Two experts argue about what one word means
Most requests go through a chain of three or more synchronous calls
Forces to split and to join conflict for one candidate
items.use: Turn each force into a business result

items.when: The upstream model is poor, old, or foreign, and your model matters
The upstream team will not change, and its model is good enough
Many consumers need the same integration
Contexts need a shared, documented exchange format, often between companies
The shared part is small, stable, and truly the same in both
The upstream team is willing and able to listen
The integration costs more than the value it gives
An old system has no clear model, and you cannot fix it now
items.use: Big ball of mud, with a boundary

items.when: The context is the core domain
items.use: Build it, and protect it with an ACL

items.when: The subdomain is generic, such as login or card payments
items.use: Buy it, and conform to it

items.when: Changes break other areas, but no part needs separate scale or releases
The packages roughly follow business areas
The code is a big ball of mud
Outside callers reach the function directly
The function is deep inside the monolith
A mistake is expensive, such as a calculation of prices or pay
The monolith has no events to publish
You select the first part to move
items.use: An edge part that fixes a problem

items.when: You move the code before the data
items.use: A plan to finish the data split

items.when: A service needs more than one copy, for load or availability
Many services are behind one public API
Work is slow or comes in peaks, and the user does not wait
Many parts react to the same event, and that list will grow
Data has relations and must stay correct
Reads are much more frequent than writes, and the primary is the limit
The same data is read many times for each write, and slightly old answers are acceptable
The system keeps large files

items.text: Make each part highly cohesive, and keep coupling between the parts low.
Shared database tables are the strongest coupling. A message that does not wait is the weakest.
Start with larger parts, and split only for a reason.
Take three likely business changes. If each usually touches one part, the boundaries are good.
A characteristic belongs to a quantum. Separate quanta let each part pay only for its needs.
Services that share one database are one quantum, however many deployments they have.
A distributed monolith has the operating cost of microservices and the change cost of a monolith.
A network call looks like a function call. It can have a third result: you do not know.
The entity trap: one component for each table leaves the business workflow with no home.
Check layer and module rules with a fitness function in each build. Without checks, they decay within months.
